rules.description: If there is no power sign and the power cable is disconnected, then the computer does not power on due to disconnected power cable.
If there is no power sign and the power button is faulty, then the computer does not power on due to a faulty power button.
If there is no power sign, the power cable is connected, and the PSU fan does not spin, then the PSU is suspected faulty.
If there is no power sign, the power cable is connected, the PSU fan spins but the motherboard standby light is off, then the motherboard or PSU may have a fault.
If the computer powers on but the monitor shows no display and the monitor is off, then the fault is the monitor being off.
If the computer powers on but shows no display, the monitor is on, and the display cable is disconnected, then the fault is a disconnected display cable.
If the computer powers on, shows no display, the monitor and cable are fine, and there are GPU beep codes, then a GPU fault is suspected.
If the computer powers on, shows no display, monitor and cable are fine, no GPU beep codes, and the RAM is not seated correctly, then a RAM seating issue causes no display.
If the system beeps on startup with a RAM-related beep code pattern and RAM is not seated correctly, then RAM is confirmed faulty or unseated.
If the system beeps on startup with a RAM-related beep code, RAM appears seated, but the system still fails, then RAM module is suspected faulty.
If there are no beep codes but the system fails to boot with RAM-related errors on screen, then RAM compatibility or failure is suspected.
If the system shuts down unexpectedly and the CPU temperature is reported as high, then overheating is the likely cause.
If the system shuts down unexpectedly, the CPU temperature is high, and the CPU fan is not spinning, then the CPU cooler fan is faulty.
If the system shuts down unexpectedly, the CPU temperature is high, the fan is spinning but thermal paste is dried out, then thermal paste replacement is required.
If the system shuts down unexpectedly and case vents are blocked, then poor airflow is causing overheating.
If the storage drive is not detected in BIOS and the data cable is disconnected, then the storage drive is not detected due to a disconnected cable.
If the storage drive is not detected in BIOS and the cable is connected but the drive makes clicking sounds, then the storage drive is likely mechanically failed.
If the system displays a boot error and the drive is detected but the OS is missing or corrupted, then the boot failure is due to corrupted OS or MBR.
If the drive is not detected and the cable is connected, no clicking sound, then the drive may have failed electronically.
If there is no power sign and neither the power cable nor power button are identified as faulty, insufficient evidence for specific diagnosis.
If the computer powers on and POST beep codes are heard and there is no video, then a POST failure has occurred — likely RAM or motherboard.
If the computer powers on, there are no POST beep codes, and the screen stays blank with no BIOS screen, this indicates a silent POST failure.
If the BIOS date resets to a default old date every boot, the CMOS battery is flat.

fault_power_cable_disconnected.label: Disconnected Power Cable
fault_power_cable_disconnected.description: The computer's main power cable is not connected to the power supply or wall outlet.
next_steps: Ensure the power cable is securely connected to the PSU and the wall outlet.
Try a different wall outlet or power strip.
If possible, try a different power cable.
fault_power_cable_disconnected.safety_note: Always power off the computer completely before reconnecting cables.

fault_power_button.label: Faulty Power Button
fault_power_button.description: The front panel power button may be stuck, broken, or disconnected from the motherboard header.
next_steps: Check if the power button feels stuck or does not click properly.
Check the motherboard front panel connector pins.
Consult a qualified technician to inspect or replace the power button.
fault_power_button.safety_note: Do not attempt to bypass the power button yourself unless you are qualified.

fault_psu_suspected.label: Suspected Power Supply Unit (PSU) Failure
fault_psu_suspected.description: The PSU fan is not spinning when power is applied, suggesting the PSU may have failed.
next_steps: Have the PSU tested by a qualified technician.
If confirmed faulty, replace the PSU with a compatible unit.
Do not open or attempt to repair a PSU yourself — it contains dangerously high voltages even when unplugged.
fault_psu_suspected.safety_note: Never open a power supply unit. It contains capacitors that hold lethal voltages even after being unplugged.

fault_motherboard_or_psu.label: Suspected Motherboard or PSU Issue
fault_motherboard_or_psu.description: The PSU fan spins but the motherboard standby light is off, indicating the motherboard may not be receiving power or may be faulty.
next_steps: Check all motherboard power connectors (24-pin ATX and 8-pin CPU).
Have a qualified technician test with a known-good PSU.
Inspect the motherboard for visible damage such as burnt components.
fault_motherboard_or_psu.safety_note: Always power off and unplug before inspecting internal components. Seek professional help for motherboard diagnosis.

fault_monitor_off.label: Monitor Not Powered On
fault_monitor_off.description: The monitor is not switched on, which is why no display is shown.
next_steps: Press the monitor's power button.
Check the monitor's power cable connection.
Verify the monitor is getting power (look for the standby LED).
fault_monitor_off.safety_note: Standard monitor operation. No safety risk.

fault_display_cable_disconnected.label: Disconnected Display Cable
fault_display_cable_disconnected.description: The cable connecting the computer to the monitor (HDMI, VGA, or DisplayPort) is not securely connected.
next_steps: Reconnect the display cable securely to both the computer and monitor.
Ensure the cable is connected to the correct port (GPU output, not motherboard if a discrete GPU is installed).
Try a different cable if available.
fault_display_cable_disconnected.safety_note: Display cables can be reconnected without powering down in most cases. However, do so carefully.

fault_gpu_suspected.label: Suspected GPU (Graphics Card) Failure
fault_gpu_suspected.description: Beep codes during startup suggest the GPU may be faulty or not seated properly.
next_steps: If the GPU is discrete, try reseating it in the PCIe slot.
Try using the motherboard's integrated graphics output (if available).
Have the GPU tested by a qualified technician.
Replace the GPU if confirmed faulty.
fault_gpu_suspected.safety_note: Power off and unplug the computer before reseating any internal components.

fault_ram_seating_no_display.label: RAM Seating Issue Causing No Display
fault_ram_seating_no_display.description: RAM modules are not correctly seated in their slots, preventing the system from passing POST and displaying anything.
next_steps: Power off and unplug the computer.
Remove the RAM modules and reinsert them firmly until the clips click.
Try booting with a single RAM stick in slot 1.
Check the motherboard manual for correct RAM slot configuration.
fault_ram_seating_no_display.safety_note: Always power off and disconnect power before touching internal components. Handle RAM by its edges.

fault_ram_unseated.label: RAM Not Properly Seated
fault_ram_unseated.description: The RAM module is not correctly inserted, causing startup beep codes and boot failure.
next_steps: Power off and unplug the computer.
Remove the RAM and reinsert it firmly until the locking clips engage.
Confirm the RAM is in the correct slot according to the motherboard manual.
Try with one stick at a time if multiple sticks are installed.
fault_ram_unseated.safety_note: Always power off and unplug before handling RAM. Ground yourself to avoid static discharge.

fault_ram_module_suspected.label: Suspected RAM Module Failure
fault_ram_module_suspected.description: RAM beep codes are present and RAM appears seated, suggesting the RAM module itself may be faulty.
next_steps: Try a different RAM module if available.
Run a memory diagnostic tool such as Windows Memory Diagnostic.
Consult a qualified technician if the problem persists.
fault_ram_module_suspected.safety_note: Power off before replacing RAM modules.

fault_ram_compatibility.label: Suspected RAM Compatibility or Failure
fault_ram_compatibility.description: RAM errors appear on screen without beep codes, suggesting a RAM compatibility or configuration issue.
next_steps: Check that the RAM speed and type (DDR4, DDR5) matches what the motherboard supports.
Check the motherboard's QVL (Qualified Vendor List) for compatible RAM.
Run Windows Memory Diagnostic to test the RAM.
fault_ram_compatibility.safety_note: Check the motherboard manual before purchasing replacement RAM.

fault_overheating_cpu.label: Suspected CPU Overheating
fault_overheating_cpu.description: The CPU is running at high temperatures, causing unexpected system shutdowns as a self-protection mechanism.
next_steps: Check that the CPU cooler is properly mounted.
Ensure case fans are working and airflow is not blocked.
Monitor CPU temperatures using a utility such as HWMonitor.
Consider replacing thermal paste or upgrading the cooler.
fault_overheating_cpu.safety_note: Do not operate the computer without proper cooling. Sustained overheating can permanently damage the CPU.

fault_cpu_fan.label: CPU Cooler Fan Not Spinning
fault_cpu_fan.description: The CPU fan is not spinning, leading to rapid overheating and automatic shutdown.
next_steps: Check that the CPU fan is connected to the CPU_FAN header on the motherboard.
Inspect for physical damage or blockage.
Replace the CPU fan or cooler if it is faulty.
fault_cpu_fan.safety_note: Never run a computer without a functioning CPU cooler. This can permanently damage the processor within minutes.

fault_thermal_paste.label: Dried or Inadequate Thermal Paste
fault_thermal_paste.description: Thermal paste between the CPU and cooler has dried out, reducing heat transfer efficiency and causing overheating.
next_steps: Have a qualified technician remove the cooler, clean off the old thermal paste, and apply a fresh application.
Use a quality thermal compound.
fault_thermal_paste.safety_note: Removing a CPU cooler requires care to avoid damaging the CPU or motherboard. Seek professional help if unsure.

fault_poor_airflow.label: Poor Case Airflow
fault_poor_airflow.description: Blocked vents or insufficient case fans are preventing adequate airflow, leading to thermal shutdowns.
next_steps: Remove any obstructions from intake and exhaust vents.
Ensure the computer is not placed in an enclosed space.
Consider adding case fans or improving cable management.
fault_poor_airflow.safety_note: Do not operate the computer in an enclosed space without adequate ventilation.

fault_storage_cable.label: Disconnected Storage Data Cable
fault_storage_cable.description: The SATA or NVMe connection to the storage drive is not properly connected, preventing detection.
next_steps: Power off and unplug the computer.
Reconnect the data cable between the storage drive and motherboard.
Also check the power cable to the drive.
Verify drive is detected in BIOS after reconnection.
fault_storage_cable.safety_note: Always power off before touching internal storage connections.

fault_storage_mechanical.label: Suspected Mechanical Hard Drive Failure
fault_storage_mechanical.description: Clicking sounds from the drive and failure to detect suggest the hard drive has a mechanical failure.
next_steps: Stop using the drive immediately to prevent further data loss.
Consult a professional data recovery service if data is important.
Replace the hard drive.
Consider switching to an SSD for better reliability.
fault_storage_mechanical.safety_note: Clicking hard drives can fail completely at any time. Back up data immediately if possible.

fault_os_boot.label: Operating System Boot Failure
fault_os_boot.description: The drive is detected but the OS or boot records are missing or corrupted, preventing Windows from starting.
next_steps: Boot from a Windows installation USB and use Startup Repair.
Use command-line tools such as bootrec /fixmbr and bootrec /fixboot.
If repair fails, consider reinstalling the operating system.
Back up data first if you can access the drive from another system.
fault_os_boot.safety_note: Reinstalling the OS will erase existing data unless data is backed up first.

fault_storage_electronic.label: Suspected Electronic Storage Drive Failure
fault_storage_electronic.description: The drive is not detected, the cable is connected, and there are no clicking sounds, suggesting an electronic failure on the drive's circuit board.
next_steps: Try the drive in a different SATA port or as an external drive in another computer.
Have a qualified technician test the drive.
If the drive has failed, consult a data recovery specialist before discarding it.
fault_storage_electronic.safety_note: Do not attempt to open a hard drive yourself — it will destroy any chance of data recovery.

fault_no_power_unknown.label: Unable to Determine Specific Power Fault
fault_no_power_unknown.description: The system shows no power but available checks did not identify a specific cause. A comprehensive hardware inspection is needed.
next_steps: Have the system inspected by a qualified technician.
Request testing of PSU, motherboard, and front panel connections.
fault_no_power_unknown.safety_note: Do not attempt internal repairs without proper training.

fault_post_failure.label: POST (Power-On Self-Test) Failure
fault_post_failure.description: The motherboard failed its startup self-test. This is typically caused by faulty or unseated RAM, a defective GPU, or a motherboard fault. The computer cannot progress past the very earliest stage of startup.
next_steps: Power off and reseat all RAM modules — remove and firmly reinsert each stick.
If multiple RAM sticks are installed, try booting with only one at a time.
Remove any recently added hardware (extra GPU, expansion cards) and test.
If the problem persists, consult a qualified technician to test the motherboard and CPU.
fault_post_failure.safety_note: Always power off and unplug the computer before reseating components. Handle RAM with care — do not touch the gold contacts.

fault_cmos_battery.label: Flat CMOS Battery
fault_cmos_battery.description: The CMOS coin cell battery on the motherboard is depleted. This battery maintains the system clock and BIOS settings when the computer is off. A flat battery causes the clock to reset to a default date on every boot.
next_steps: Purchase a CR2032 coin cell battery (widely available and inexpensive).
Power off and unplug the computer.
Locate the coin cell battery on the motherboard and replace it.
After replacement, set the correct date and time in BIOS.
fault_cmos_battery.safety_note: CMOS battery replacement is safe and straightforward, but always unplug the computer first and avoid touching other components unnecessarily.
